newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: BOE says S.African rate cut still likely this year.
newsitem.headline: BOE says S.African rate cut still likely this year.

text.p: A cut in the bank rate was still possible this year with at least two more in 1998, Board of Executors economist Rob Lee said on Thursday.
In his latest Investment Outlook, Lee said commentators who seemed to be ruling out more than marginal cuts in short term rates in 1997 and 1998 were "too pessimistic".
But a cut in the Bank rate, currently 17 percent, was not imminent as it would be a few months before there was clear evidence of the desired cooling off of the economy.
"Furthermore, the Reserve Bank will want to assess the impact of the exchange control relaxations that take effect in July," Lee said.
"Providing that the government continues to move ahead in the economic reform process, capital inflows should comfortably accommodate likely outflows.
"We therefore still expect a cut in the Bank rate before year-end and see every possibility of at least two more reductions in 1998."
Lee said that as the risks of investing in South Africa were seen to diminish, the current high levels of real short term interest rates would no longer be necessary.
For example, he said, a real prime overdraft rate of nine percent in 1998 would still be well above historic or international norms.
"Yet if the inflation rate were to average seven percent next year, which seems plausible, this would then imply a nominal prime rate four percent lower than at present."
Prime lending rates currently stand at 20.25 percent.

Reserve Bank governor Chris Stals last week fuelled the debate about the direction of monetary policy when he said that recent trends in monetary and credit growth and inflation "beg the question whether monetary policy at this juncture is restrictive enough."
This was seen as signalling that the central bank might be considering further interest rate hikes rather than the hoped for reduction.

Lee said that although the growth in broad money supply (M3) and credit was disappointing, it appeared as if this had been caused by extensive switching from offshore to local sources of finance following the withdrawal of the Reserve Bank from the foward cover market.
This switch was due to the fact that the cost of forward cover from banks was higher than from the Reserve Bank.

"There is therefore an important structural increase in the demand for domestic credit underway which cannot be considered inflationary because it does not represent a new source of demand in the economy," Lee said.

At the same time, the demand for consumer credit appeared soft, the growth in notes and coins in circulation (MO) had started falling last year and initial estimates of a surge in retail sales in January had been revised downwards.
At the same time, employment growth remained weak and there was no evidence of a surge in the level of wage increases in recent months.
Much now depended on government being able to meet its ambitious targets to keep its consumption expenditure down and investors would be watching initial figures like hawks, Lee said.
All these factors indicated encouraging evidence that the economy was cooling down, providing scope for an interest rate cut later in the year.
-- Lynda Loxton, Cape Town newsroom +27 21 25-2238
